pr.title: Exit quietly when the reader of the output goes away
pr.head: bac28ba21ed4574b360d2edf3b7d1f88b2585283

summary: Every project command writes its results to standard output, and people often pipe that output into another program, such as project show big | head -4. When that reader exits early, the next write to the pipe fails with BrokenPipeError, the error Python raises when nothing reads the other end of a pipe any more.

Before this change, that showed up two ways. A write that failed while the command ran was caught by the CLI's general OSError handler, which printed project: [Errno 32] Broken pipe and exited 65, the status that otherwise means invalid project data. Output still sitting in Python's buffer when the command finished failed only in the interpreter's own flush at exit, which printed Exception ignored while flushing sys.stdout and exited 120.

Now main flushes standard output itself, catches BrokenPipeError, points standard output at the null device so nothing is left to fail at exit, and returns 141. That is 128 plus the number of SIGPIPE, the signal a closed pipe sends, and it is the status a shell reports when cat or git stops the same way. Every other error is reported exactly as before.

The change keeps Python's default of ignoring SIGPIPE rather than letting the signal kill the process. A killed process could stop in the middle of a write that has to land whole, such as an update to the inbox store, while an exception unwinds through the code's own cleanup.

groups.title: Catching the closed pipe in main
groups.kicker: Where the CLI turns a closed reader into a silent exit with status 141
intro: The old main becomes run_command, which runs the command and turns each error into a message on standard error and an exit status. It now lets BrokenPipeError pass up instead of reporting it as an OSError, because BrokenPipeError is a kind of OSError and would otherwise land in that handler.

The new main calls run_command, then flushes standard output with flush_stdout, so output still in Python's buffer fails here, where the code can catch it, rather than in the interpreter's flush at exit, where it cannot. On BrokenPipeError it uses os.dup2 to point standard output's file descriptor at the null device, so the flush at exit writes the rest of the buffer somewhere harmless, and returns 141.
parse flushes too, because argparse's --help and --version print and then raise SystemExit, which leaves through parse without reaching the flush in main.

checks.text: Only a closed standard output or standard error reaches the new handler. Each subprocess write in the CLI goes through subprocess.run(input=…), which ignores a closed child's pipe itself, and the two urlopen calls catch OSError where they are made. Checked by reading every subprocess and network call in src/projector.

A command that changes state is no more likely to stop halfway than before: the exception is raised at the same point as on the base, and only how it is reported changes. Running project status big ready | true wrote the new status and exited 141, so a script never sees success for output nobody read.

files.note: Splits the old main into run_command and a new main that flushes standard output and handles BrokenPipeError.

checks.text: raise here keeps BrokenPipeError out of the OSError handler below it, which would otherwise print the error and return 65.
A genuine error still surfaces: project show nosuch | head prints project not found and exits 66, and test_another_os_error_is_still_reported checks that another OSError still prints and exits 65.
sys.stdout is None when the command starts with standard output already closed, so both this line and flush_stdout check for it. A test runs show that way and expects status 0.

groups.title: Tests and documentation
groups.kicker: Real pipes in subprocesses, a reworked inbox test, and the exit-code table
intro: The failed flush at exit happens after every handler in the program has run, so only a separate process shows it. ClosedReaderTests therefore runs the CLI as a subprocess, both ways it is installed: as python -m projector and as the console script, which calls projector.cli:main directly.

The inbox test for inbox watch used to swap in a fake stream that raised the error. It now writes to a real pipe whose reading end is closed, because main needs a real file descriptor to redirect. watch still marks an answer delivered only after its line is flushed, so an answer it could not print waits for the next deliverer.

checks.text: With the base cli.py and this head's tests, six subtests of ClosedReaderTests fail; with this head all pass. The whole suite, 1031 tests, passes under Python 3.12.

files.note: Adds ClosedReaderTests: a reader that stops after one line, a reader gone before any output, a reader that reads everything, standard output closed from the start, and another OSError.
The inbox watch test now expects 141 and an empty standard error, and writes to a real closed pipe.
